summary: Defines the XML Configuration Access Protocol, which lets a client read, write and modify application configuration data stored in XML on a server. It maps document parts and attributes to HTTP URIs.

plainLanguage.summary: XCAP is a way to read and change XML files that a server keeps on behalf of a user. It gives every part of such a file an address, so a program can fetch one element, change one attribute or replace a whole document with an ordinary web request.

subtitle: Reading and editing XML configuration on a server with ordinary HTTP requests.

tldr.problem: Servers need per-user settings that the user keeps, such as a list of friends or a set of rules about who may see their status, and those settings have to be editable from a phone, a browser or a desktop program.
tldr.mechanism: XCAP maps parts of an XML document to HTTP URIs, so a document, an element inside it, or a single attribute can be fetched, written or deleted with the ordinary GET, PUT and DELETE methods.
tldr.outcome: Any application can store its own XML configuration on the same server and let any HTTP client edit it, with the rules for naming, validation and permissions defined once per application.

today: RFC 4825 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and the application usages it was written for, such as the resource lists document format, are separate documents.

sections.title: What Problem XCAP Solves
sections.content:
Many communications applications need the network servers to reach per-user information while servicing a request. That information sits inside the network, but the end user manages it, and the user manages it from several places: a web page, a wireless handset or a desktop program. Examples are the presence authorization policy, which says which watchers may subscribe to a presentity and what they may see, and presence lists, which name the users whose presence a watcher wants.

XCAP is the protocol for manipulating that per-user data. It is a set of conventions for mapping XML documents and their components into HTTP URIs, rules for how a change to one resource affects another, data validation constraints, and authorization policies for access to those resources. Because the result is built on that structure, ordinary HTTP primitives do the work.

The document is explicit about what XCAP is not. It was not designed as a general-purpose XML search protocol, as an XML database update protocol, or as a general-purpose XML-based configuration protocol for network elements. It borrows ideas from the Application Configuration Access Protocol, RFC 2244, but it is not an extension of that protocol and does not depend on it.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers often need settings that belong to a user, such as a list of friends or rules about who may see the user's status. The user edits them from a phone or a browser. XCAP is the set of rules that lets those settings be stored as XML on a server and edited with web requests.

sections.title: How the Pieces Fit Together
sections.content:
Each application that uses XCAP defines an application usage, which sets out the XML schema for its data along with other key information. The main task of XCAP is to let clients read, write, modify, create and delete pieces of that data, and it does so over HTTP/1.1.

The XCAP server acts as a repository for collections of XML documents. There are documents for each application, and within each application there are documents for each user, and a user can have several documents for one application. To reach a component of one of those documents, XCAP defines an algorithm for building a URI that names it. A component means any element or attribute inside the document, so the URIs point at a document or at something finer grained than the document itself. An HTTP resource that follows the naming conventions and validation constraints of XCAP is called an XCAP resource.

Because XCAP resources are HTTP resources, they are used with HTTP methods: GET reads one, PUT creates or modifies one, and DELETE removes one. POST is not defined, because an XCAP resource does not represent a processing script. The properties HTTP associates with resources apply, and entity tags in particular are useful here because they let a client make a change conditional on the document not having changed in the meantime.

Two XML documents that are equivalent for the purposes of an application may look different on the wire. With XCAP resources, the canonical form of an XML document decides what counts as equivalent, which is what fixes how significant whitespace is and means that a new attribute may appear in any order in the physical representation.
sections.plainLanguage: The server keeps XML files for each application and for each user of that application. XCAP gives every file, and every element and attribute inside it, an address. A client then uses the usual web methods: GET to read, PUT to write, DELETE to remove.

sections.title: What an Application Usage Must Say
sections.content:
An application usage is what makes a set of XML documents usable by one application. It defines the schema of the data, the well-known URIs used to reach it, and several other things.

Each application usage has a name, the Application Unique ID, which tells apart the resources of one application from those of another. There are two namespaces for these names. The IETF namespace holds tokens registered with IANA as standards-track documents are published. The vendor namespace holds names built from the reverse domain name of the organisation, followed by a period and a vendor token, so the example.com domain can create com.example.foo but not org.example.foo. Names in the vendor namespace need no registration, which is what makes them useful in a laboratory.

Every application usage must also define a default document namespace. That is the namespace assumed for elements in a URI that carry no prefix. It applies only when a URI is being evaluated, not to the documents themselves, which is why the document distinguishes it from the ordinary XML default namespace.

Validation is the responsibility of the server. The application usage must describe its documents with an XML schema and name the MIME type for documents that follow it, and it must state any further constraints, since a schema cannot express everything. Uniqueness constraints are the most important of these: the usage says which field or combination of fields must be unique and within what scope, for example that the name attribute of a list element must be unique among the children of one parent. URI constraints on the shape of a URI cannot be expressed in a schema and must be written out. Referential integrity is different again: an application usage may state it, but the server does not enforce it, because an XCAP server is not a database. The client is responsible for making the changes that keep such references correct. All documents used with XCAP must be encoded in UTF-8, and no application usage may change that.

An application usage also states the authorization policy. The default policy is that each user may read, change and delete every document below their own home directory, that any user may read the documents in the global tree, and that only users explicitly trusted by the server operator may change global documents. An application usage may replace that policy, and may name another application usage to hold the policies.
sections.plainLanguage: Each application tells the server what its files look like: the schema, the file type, the rules about what must be unique, and who is allowed to read or change what. The server checks the rules on every write, except for rules about links between files, which are the client's job.

sections.title: How the URI Is Built
sections.content:
An XCAP URI is the XCAP root, then the document selector, then the node selector separator, then the percent-encoded form of the node selector, and finally an optional query component that carries the namespace bindings used when the URI is evaluated.

The XCAP root is the context in which every other resource exists. It is written as an HTTP URI, but it points at nothing on the server; it names the root of the tree where the documents are kept. It must not contain a query component, and it is recommended that it has the form xcap.domain, where domain is the provider's domain. A client that has not been told otherwise should assume that form, using the domain of its own service, which for SIP means the domain part of its address of record. The root URI is normally provisioned into the client. A server may support several root URIs, in which case it behaves as if it were serving separate domains, with no information carried between them. The root URI may also be relative, in which case the application usage has to name the base URI for any XCAP URI that appears inside a document.

The document selector is a sequence of path segments separated by slashes that organizes the documents. The first segment must be the application unique ID, so all the documents of the resource lists application sit under /resource-lists. Beneath that there are two sub-trees: global, for documents that apply to every user, and users, for documents that belong to one user. The segment after the application unique ID must be one of those two. Under users there are one or more sub-trees, one per user, named by the XCAP User Identifier; for SIP systems it is recommended that this be the address of record, so a client that knows its address of record also knows its identifier. Characters that a SIP URI allows but an HTTP path segment does not, such as ? and /, must be percent-encoded. The sub-tree of one user is that user's home directory. The rest of the document selector names the documents, and the last segment is the equivalent of a file name, which for a user with a single document should be index. Subdirectories are permitted but not recommended, since XCAP has no way to create them or list their contents.

The node selector separator is a single path segment of two tilde characters. It should not be percent-encoded, and a URI that writes it as %7E%7E is equivalent. It is the boundary between the document selector and the node selector, and because a node selector may itself contain two tildes, the first pair in the URI is the separator.
sections.plainLanguage: The address of an XCAP file has three parts: the server's root address, the path to the file inside the tree of applications and users, and, after two tildes, the path to one element or attribute inside that file.

sections.title: The Language of Node Selectors
sections.content:
A node selector names an element, an attribute, or a set of namespace bindings inside a document. It is written as a sequence of steps separated by slashes, optionally followed by a terminal selector for an attribute or for the namespace bindings.

Each step chooses one element. The server starts at the root of the document and enumerates the children of the current element in document order. It discards the ones whose name does not match, where the name may be a wildcard that keeps them all. It then applies the predicates in the square brackets, in order. A position predicate keeps the element at that position and discards the rest, and if the list is shorter than the position the result is no match. An attribute predicate keeps the elements that carry that attribute with that value, and again the result is no match when there are none. A namespace declaration cannot be used as a predicate, because a namespace node is not an attribute, so a step such as el-name[@xmlns='namespace'] never matches anything.

After the predicates, the result must be exactly one element. If it is nothing, or more than one, the node selector is invalid, and the same applies to a step that matches several elements. That is stricter than XPath, where a context may hold several nodes.

The last step may instead be a terminal selector. An attribute selector picks the attribute with that expanded name from the element reached, or gives no match if there is none. The namespace selector returns the set of namespace bindings in scope for that element, including the default namespace declaration, which the server can send back in a form the client can read. Comments, text and processing instructions cannot be selected on their own, although they are returned when an element that encloses them is selected. Whitespace is respected: if a client writes whitespace into a document, the server keeps it and gives it back unchanged.

Names are matched after expansion, which turns any prefix into the namespace URI it stands for. The prefixes come from the query component of the URI, and an element with no prefix takes the default document namespace of the application usage, while an attribute with no prefix is in no namespace at all. The node selector borrows its concepts from XPath, and before percent-encoding it happens to be a valid XPath expression, but XPath offers far more than XCAP needs and the extra breadth would only add complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: The path inside a file works like a list of instructions: take the children of the current element, keep the ones with a given name, then keep only the one at a given position or with a given attribute value. Every step must end at exactly one element, or the address is invalid.

sections.title: What a Client Does
sections.content:
An XCAP client is an HTTP/1.1 client, and every operation is a method with the right headers. Before changing anything the client should check that the result would still meet the constraints of the application usage, including the schema, because the server rejects a document that breaks them with a 409 response. That response may carry an XML body that describes the error, and the client may use it to change the request, but it should not simply repeat the same request.

The client must also keep the HTTP rule that PUT and DELETE are idempotent: repeating a PUT leaves the same document, and a second DELETE finds nothing. The document expresses this as GET(PUT(x)) equals x, which in practice means that after a PUT the address used must point at the resource just written, and after a DELETE it must point at nothing. A request that breaks this is rejected with a 409 and a cannot-insert error.

To create or replace a document, the client sends a PUT to the document URI with the MIME type named by the application usage, for example application/rls-services+xml and not application/xml. To delete a document it sends a DELETE, and to fetch one it sends a GET. Elements and attributes work the same way. To create or replace an element, the client sends a PUT whose address carries a node selector and whose body is the element, with the content type application/xcap-el+xml. If the selector matches nothing in the current document the server creates the element, and if it matches an element the server replaces it completely, including its attributes, namespace declarations and content. A client that wants to insert an element at a particular place among its siblings uses a selector of the form parent/*[position][unique-attribute-value], where the second predicate makes the selector match nothing today, so that the PUT inserts rather than replaces. Deleting an element uses a DELETE whose selector matches the element and matches nothing after the removal. Fetching an element or an attribute uses a GET, and an attribute is fetched as an application/xcap-att+xml document. The namespace bindings in scope for an element can be fetched with the namespace selector, which returns application/xcap-ns+xml.

Two limits follow from the idempotency rule. An element cannot be replaced if the selector used to find it relies on the very attribute whose value is being changed, because the selector would no longer match afterwards. The way round it is to select by position instead, or to send the parent element with the child replaced inside it.

Conditional requests use the If-Match and If-None-Match headers with the entity tag. A client that has cached a document can ask the server to refuse the change if the document has changed since, in which case the server answers 412 and the client fetches the document again and retries. A conditional GET with If-None-Match returns 304 when the client's copy is still current. All the resources inside one document share one entity tag, so the tag returned after a change to one element can be used for a conditional request about another.
sections.plainLanguage: Reading is a GET, writing is a PUT, deleting is a DELETE, and the address says whether the client means a whole file, one element or one attribute. One rule shapes everything: after the write, fetching the same address must give back what was written, so the server refuses requests that would break that.

sections.title: What the Server Does
sections.content:
The XCAP server is an HTTP/1.1 origin server. It must be explicitly configured for each application usage it handles, and it must know the constraints that usage imposes.

The order of work is fixed. If the URI names an application usage the server does not understand, a user it does not recognise, or an extension selector it does not understand, the request is rejected with 404. The server then authenticates the request: every XCAP server must implement HTTP Digest authentication, and must implement HTTP over TLS. It then checks that the client is allowed to perform the operation, using the policies of the application usage. After that it checks the URI itself: it splits the URI at the first pair of tildes, and if the node selector uses a namespace prefix that the query component does not define, the request is rejected with 400. A POST to an XCAP resource should be answered with 405.

For a PUT, the server first locates the parent, which is the URI with its last path segment removed. That parent may be a document, an element, or a directory in the document tree. If the parent does not exist, the server answers 409 and should include a conflict report naming the no-parent condition. If the parent exists, the server checks whether a document of that name is already there, which makes the operation a replacement rather than a creation.

A 409 response usually carries a body that says what went wrong, in the application/xcap-error+xml format. The root element is xcap-error, and the child element names the condition: not-well-formed for a body that is not well-formed XML, not-xml-frag for a body that should have been an XML fragment, no-parent for a missing parent, schema-validation-error for a document that no longer matches its schema, cannot-insert for a PUT that would break idempotency, cannot-delete for a DELETE that would, uniqueness-failure for a value that is not unique, which carries the field at fault and may suggest alternative values, constraint-failure for any other rule of the application usage, not-utf-8 for an encoding problem, and extension for conditions defined elsewhere.

The server must keep an entity tag for every resource it holds, with one rule on top of the normal ones: when anything in a document changes, every resource in that document gets the same new tag, so a document effectively has a single tag. The Etag header must be included in every 200 or 201 response to a PUT, GET or DELETE, as long as the document still exists afterwards.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks the request in a fixed order: does it understand this application and this user, is the client who it says it is, is it allowed to do this, and does the address make sense. When something fails it answers with a code such as 404 or 409, and a 409 comes with an XML body that names the problem.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The data XCAP handles is often sensitive, because it includes the settings that decide what a service may do on behalf of a user and for whom. An administrator is therefore recommended to hand out an HTTPS URI as the XCAP root URI, which encrypts the traffic between client and server and stops anyone listening from reading it. Clients must implement TLS so that such addresses work.

Authentication matters in both directions. A client needs to be sure it is talking to the server it believes it is, otherwise it can be fed false information, which can be turned into a denial-of-service attack against the client, so a client should upgrade a connection to TLS. Authorizing reads and writes depends on knowing who the client is, so a server should challenge the client with HTTP Digest authentication, and should do that over TLS. Clients must implement digest authentication so that they interoperate with servers that use it, and a server must not use basic authentication without a TLS connection.

One difficulty comes from XCAP being a usage of HTTP rather than a separate protocol: it runs on the same port numbers as ordinary HTTP traffic, so a firewall cannot separate XCAP traffic from other web traffic by port. The document notes that this is a general problem with HTTP, and that separating the two would require the firewall to look at the address itself. The presence of the double tilde is a strong hint that an address points at an element or an attribute, but there is no foolproof way to tell, and the many ways a URI can be encoded on the wire make the check harder still.
sections.plainLanguage: The files XCAP edits often contain private settings, so the traffic should be encrypted and the client should prove who it is. Digest authentication over TLS is the answer the document gives. One limit is that XCAP shares the web ports, so a firewall that wants to block it has to look at the address rather than the port.
